standards.SEV1: Flow of energy and cycling of matter within an ecosystem
standards.SEV2: Stability and change in Earth's ecosystems
standards.SEV3: Types, availability, allocation, and sustainability of energy resources
standards.SEV5: Effects of human population growth on global ecosystems

elements.SEV1b: Laws of Thermodynamics & energy transfer (food chains/webs, trophic levels, 10% rule)
elements.SEV1c: Biogeochemical cycles (water, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, oxygen)
elements.SEV1d: Physical factors & organismal adaptations in terrestrial biomes
elements.SEV1e: Chemical & physical properties of Georgia aquatic biomes
elements.SEV2a: Short- & long-term natural climate fluctuations (El Niño, volcanism, Milankovitch)
elements.SEV2b: Atmospheric chemistry (CO₂, methane) & the greenhouse effect
elements.SEV2d: Value of biodiversity in ecosystem resilience
elements.SEV3a: Origin & consumption of renewable & non-renewable energy
elements.SEV3d: Design & defend a sustainable energy plan for a location
elements.SEV4a: Effects of human activities on natural resources
elements.SEV4b: Solutions to reduce human impact (smog, ozone, urbanization, ocean acidification)
elements.SEV4c: Human population growth vs. food demand/supply (GMOs, monoculture, desertification, Green Revolution)
elements.SEV5a: Quality of life & human impact (population growth, education, GNP)
elements.SEV5b: Global population patterns (fertility/mortality, demographic transition, pyramids)
elements.SEV5c: Ecological effects of human innovations (Ag, Industrial, Medical, Technological)

items.stem: All of the white-tailed deer living in Red Top Mountain State Park make up which level of biological organization?
options: A whole community
An entire ecosystem
A population
A single organism

diagnoses.0: Thinks a single-species group is a 'community' rather than a population.

items.stem: Which level of organization includes BOTH the living and the non-living parts of an area?
options: An ecosystem
A single organism
A community
A population

diagnoses.2: Believes only the biotic (living) components make up an ecosystem.

items.stem: Every largemouth bass living in one Georgia farm pond represents which level of biological organization?
options: An entire ecosystem
The whole biosphere
A population
A whole community

diagnoses.3: Thinks a single-species group is a 'community' rather than a population.

items.stem: A student says an ecosystem is made of only the living things in an area. What is the student leaving out?
options: The non-living (abiotic) factors, like water and soil
Nothing important — that definition is complete
The populations living in the nearby neighboring ecosystems
The smallest microscopic organisms in the soil

diagnoses.1: Believes only the biotic (living) components make up an ecosystem.

items.stem: A producer level in a food chain contains 10,000 kcal of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy is available to the SECONDARY consumers?
options: About 1,000 kcal
About 10 kcal
About 100 kcal
About 9,000 kcal

diagnoses.3: Thinks 90% (not 10%) of energy passes to the next trophic level.

items.stem: As energy moves up a food chain, about 90% is not passed to the next level. What happens to that energy?
options: It travels back down the chain to be reused later
It is stored permanently in the bodies of producers
It is released as heat the next level cannot use
It is destroyed and leaves the ecosystem entirely

diagnoses.3: Believes energy 'lost' between trophic levels is destroyed (violates the 1st Law).

items.stem: Grass in a field stores 50,000 kcal of energy. Following the 10% rule, about how much energy reaches the primary consumers (grasshoppers)?
options: About 500 kcal
About 5,000 kcal
About 45,000 kcal
About 50,000 kcal

diagnoses.2: Thinks 90% (not 10%) of energy passes to the next trophic level.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes matter and energy in an ecosystem?
options: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat; matter cycles
Both energy and matter are destroyed at each level
Both energy and matter are recycled endlessly
Matter flows away as heat while energy keeps cycling

diagnoses.2: Believes energy is recycled like matter rather than flowing one way.

items.target: Role of microbes in the nitrogen cycle
items.stem: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas (N₂) directly from the air. What makes nitrogen available to plants?
options: Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into forms plants absorb
Plants breathe in nitrogen gas through their leaves
Lightning instantly turns all nitrogen gas into oxygen
Plants manufacture their own nitrogen from sunlight

diagnoses.1: Thinks plants obtain usable nitrogen by 'breathing it in' rather than through microbial fixation.

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and stores carbon in living tissue?
options: Cellular respiration
Photosynthesis
Decomposition
Combustion of fuels

diagnoses.0: Reverses photosynthesis and respiration in the carbon cycle.

items.stem: Why does phosphorus move differently through its cycle than carbon and nitrogen do?
options: Phosphorus is found only dissolved in the deep ocean
Phosphorus is not really needed by living things at all
Phosphorus rarely enters the air; it stays in rock and soil
Phosphorus is a gas that stays mostly in the air

diagnoses.1: Believes only some cycles matter to life; overlooks phosphorus in DNA, ATP, etc.

items.stem: A student claims the water, carbon, and nitrogen cycles each work completely on their own. Why is this incorrect?
options: The cycles connect; matter moves among them as it cycles
It is correct — each cycle runs fully on its own
The cycles interact only deep inside animal bodies
Only the water cycle actually moves real matter around

diagnoses.1: Believes the biogeochemical cycles are completely independent of one another.

items.stem: Desert cacti store water in thick stems and have a waxy coating. These adaptations are mainly a response to which physical factors?
options: Cold, salty breezes blowing off a nearby ocean
Intense sunlight and very little available water
Deep, shady soil that is very rich in nutrients
Heavy rainfall and consistently cool temperatures

diagnoses.2: Attributes adaptations to soil/biotic factors rather than the controlling abiotic factors.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why organisms living far inland often differ from those living near a coastline?
options: Distance from the ocean changes moisture and temperature
Only the other animals present determine adaptations
Coastlines have no measurable effect on any organisms
Inland and coastal organisms are always identical

diagnoses.1: Believes there is little or no relationship between abiotic factors and adaptations.

items.stem: Rocky Mountain goats have hard, split hooves and are extremely sure-footed. Which physical factor most directly shaped this adaptation?
options: The number of daylight hours in each season
The amount of nitrogen found in the local soil
The steep, rocky terrain they climb (topography)
How close their home range sits to the ocean coastline

diagnoses.3: Selects an abiotic factor unrelated to the described adaptation.

items.stem: A camel is well adapted to shifting sand and long dry periods but would struggle on steep, rocky cliffs. This shows that:
options: Every environment requires the exact same adaptations
Adaptations are random and unrelated to the environment
Physical (abiotic) factors shape which adaptations help
Adaptations depend only on the other animals present

diagnoses.3: Believes only biotic factors drive adaptation.
diagnoses.1: Believes adaptations are unrelated to environmental conditions.

items.stem: A healthy Georgia stream usually has dissolved oxygen (DO) between 5 and 8 ppm. Why does dissolved oxygen matter?
options: It steadily makes the water much more acidic over time
Organisms get all their oxygen from the water molecules
It raises the turbidity and cloudiness of the water
Fish and other aquatic organisms need it to breathe

diagnoses.1: Believes oxygen is unimportant to aquatic life because organisms get it from H₂O molecules.

items.stem: Scientists collect many mayfly, stonefly, and caddisfly larvae (sensitive species) from a stream. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Nothing at all can be inferred about the water
The water contains almost no dissolved oxygen at all
The water is heavily polluted and low in oxygen
The water is healthy with plenty of dissolved oxygen

diagnoses.2: Confuses sensitive (pollution-intolerant) species with tolerant, pollution-loving species.

items.stem: Which measurement tells a scientist how cloudy (how much suspended material is in) stream water?
options: The dissolved oxygen
The temperature
The pH level
The turbidity

diagnoses.2: Confuses acidity/basicity with cloudiness of water.

items.stem: Which macroinvertebrate sample best indicates a HEALTHY Georgia stream?
options: A huge number of just one single very tolerant species
Only tolerant aquatic worms and mosquito larvae
A diverse mix that includes sensitive mayfly larvae
No living macroinvertebrates of any kind present

diagnoses.0: Equates abundance of one tolerant species with good water quality rather than diversity.

items.target: Volcanism as a short-term climate driver
items.stem: The 1991 eruption of Mt. Pinatubo temporarily lowered Earth's average temperature by about 0.5°C. Why?
options: Ash and gases blocked some incoming sunlight
It permanently changed Earth's orbit around the Sun
The volcano added extra oxygen to the atmosphere
Flowing lava warmed the world's oceans everywhere

diagnoses.1: Confuses a short-term event with long-term orbital (Milankovitch) change.

items.stem: Which is an example of a LONG-term natural cause of climate change (acting over tens of thousands of years)?
options: Milankovitch cycles in Earth's orbit and tilt
One large volcanic eruption that blocks sunlight
A single record-breaking summer heat wave
A single strong El Niño event in the Pacific

diagnoses.3: Classifies a short-term (2–7 year) fluctuation as a long-term driver.

items.target: El Niño is a natural, recurring fluctuation
items.stem: During an El Niño event, the trade winds weaken or reverse. El Niño typically occurs:
options: Only once every few million years or so
Every 2–7 years, with no fixed schedule
Every single year on exactly the same date
Only when human air pollution triggers it

diagnoses.3: Believes all climate change is caused by humans.

items.stem: A student says climates can never change unless humans cause it. Which evidence best corrects this idea?
options: Only factories, cars, and power plants change climate
Natural events changed climate long before humans
Climate change is not actually real at all
Climates truly never change on their own

diagnoses.3: Believes climates cannot change.
diagnoses.0: Believes climate change is always due to human impact.

items.stem: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane affect Earth's temperature by:
options: Blocking all incoming sunlight from the surface
Trapping heat energy near Earth's surface
Reflecting all heat into space to cool the planet
Producing extra oxygen for living things to use

diagnoses.2: Believes greenhouse gases cool the planet rather than trap heat.

items.target: Greenhouse gases are natural and necessary
items.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases is TRUE?
options: They are entirely human-made and unnatural
They occur naturally and keep Earth warm enough
They exist only in the air and nowhere else
They have no real effect on Earth's temperature

diagnoses.0: Believes greenhouse gases are not a natural part of Earth's atmosphere.
diagnoses.2: Believes greenhouse gases exist only in the atmosphere (ignores sinks/organisms).

items.stem: Data show that atmospheric CO₂ and average global temperature both rose over the same time period. This pattern is best described as:
options: Showing no relationship between the two trends
Proof the air contains no greenhouse gases at all
Proof that temperature follows no real pattern
A sign the two rising trends may be connected

diagnoses.0: Fails to recognize a correlation between greenhouse gases and temperature.

items.stem: Besides releasing gases, what else can increase the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere?
options: Nothing besides direct emissions can change it
Cutting down forests that absorb carbon dioxide
Somehow increasing the size of the oceans
Planting many millions more forests around the world

diagnoses.0: Thinks only emissions — not the loss of sinks — change atmospheric CO₂.

items.stem: Which situation would begin PRIMARY succession?
options: Bare rock left behind after a glacier retreats
A flooded meadow that keeps its rich topsoil
An old farm field that still has all its soil
A forest regrowing after a wildfire, on soil

diagnoses.3: Confuses secondary succession (soil remains) with primary succession.

items.stem: As an ecosystem moves through succession toward a climax community, biomass and biodiversity generally:
options: Disappear completely
Stay exactly the same
Steadily decrease
Steadily increase

diagnoses.1: Believes biodiversity is not part of succession.

items.stem: Lichens and mosses are often the first organisms to colonize bare rock after a disturbance. These are called:
options: A climax community
Pioneer species
Invasive species
Keystone species

diagnoses.0: Confuses the first colonizers with the final, stable climax stage.

items.stem: A student says every climax community looks the same and always takes thousands of years to form. What is the best correction?
options: The student's statement is completely correct
Deserts and forests reach identical climax communities
Climax communities vary by biome and can form faster
Succession never actually reaches a climax community

diagnoses.0: Believes succession always takes thousands of years and all climax communities are the same.
diagnoses.1: Believes all climax communities look the same regardless of biome.

items.stem: The gopher tortoise digs burrows that many other Georgia species use for shelter and to escape fire. The gopher tortoise is best described as a:
options: A non-native species
An invasive species
A keystone species
A pioneer species

diagnoses.1: Confuses a native species others depend on with a harmful introduced species.

items.stem: Why does higher biodiversity usually make an ecosystem more stable and resilient?
options: It doesn't — biodiversity has no effect on stability
Only the very largest species affect its stability
Other species can fill a role when one declines
More species always cause an ecosystem to collapse

diagnoses.0: Believes biodiversity does not make an ecosystem more stable.

items.stem: Kudzu was introduced to the southeastern United States and now grows over and outcompetes native plants. Kudzu is an example of a(n):
options: An invasive species
A keystone species
An endemic species
An indicator species

diagnoses.2: Confuses a spreading introduced species with one found only in a single place.

items.target: Not all non-native species are invasive
items.stem: Which statement about non-native species is correct?
options: Every non-native species eventually becomes invasive
The terms 'native' and 'non-native' mean the same
Non-native species are always helpful to an ecosystem
Only some non-native species become invasive

diagnoses.0: Believes all non-native species end up being invasive species.

items.stem: Which of the following is a NON-renewable energy source?
options: Solar power
Coal
Wind power
Geothermal

diagnoses.2: Misclassifies a renewable source as non-renewable.

items.target: Why nuclear is grouped as non-renewable
items.stem: Why is nuclear power usually grouped with the non-renewable sources?
options: Because it depends on limited uranium fuel
Because it uses fast-flowing river water
Because it runs directly on sunlight
Because it never produces any waste

diagnoses.2: Believes nuclear power is a renewable energy source.

items.stem: Which list contains ONLY renewable energy sources?
options: Coal, oil, natural gas
Uranium, coal, solar
Natural gas, wind, oil
Solar, wind, hydropower

diagnoses.1: Includes a non-renewable fuel (uranium/coal) among 'renewables'.

items.stem: According to U.S. energy data, which source provided the LARGEST share of U.S. energy in 2021?
options: Solar power
Geothermal
Wind power
Fossil fuels

diagnoses.0: Assumes all energy sources are used in roughly equal amounts.

items.stem: Which of these is a genuine BENEFIT of solar energy?
options: It runs on uranium fuel rods, like a reactor
It emits large amounts of CO₂ during use
It works just as well at night as in daytime
It is renewable and pollutes little while running

diagnoses.2: Overlooks that solar output depends on sunlight/daylight.

items.stem: A student claims renewable energy sources have no drawbacks at all. Which is a REAL drawback of a renewable source?
options: They run out quickly, just like fossil fuels do
Solar and wind depend on weather and daylight
They release the most greenhouse gases of any
Renewables genuinely have no drawbacks at all

diagnoses.3: Believes renewable energy sources have no risks or drawbacks.

items.stem: Which is a real BENEFIT of fossil fuels compared with many renewable sources?
options: They are reliable and easy to store and move
They can never be used up or run out
They produce no pollution at all when burned
They are a fully renewable energy source

diagnoses.3: Believes fossil fuels are renewable.

items.stem: Which of these is a genuine RISK of nuclear power?
options: It carries no real risks of any kind
It creates long-lived radioactive waste
It depends entirely on the daily weather
It emits large amounts of CO₂ while running

diagnoses.3: Believes nuclear generation emits large amounts of CO₂.

items.stem: Being 'renewable' does NOT automatically make an energy source 'sustainable.' Which example shows this?
options: Solar panels last forever and use no materials
Sunlight will completely run out within a year
Wind power is actually a non-renewable resource
Biofuels can require soil-depleting monoculture farms

diagnoses.0: Assumes renewable sources have no material or land costs.

items.stem: To decide whether an energy source is sustainable, scientists should consider:
options: Its full impact from collection to disposal
Only whether the source is currently popular
Only how modern the technology looks today
Only how much the source costs us today

diagnoses.3: Believes sustainability only concerns present-day cost/our lifetime.

items.target: Why nuclear is judged not fully sustainable
items.stem: Despite its low emissions, why is nuclear power often judged NOT fully sustainable?
options: Because it releases large amounts of CO₂
Because its radioactive waste lasts a very long time
Because it uses up far too much sunlight
Because it is completely harmless to use

diagnoses.0: Believes nuclear generation is a major CO₂ source.

items.stem: Which question best helps evaluate whether an energy plan is sustainable?
options: Can it last long-term without doing major harm?
Does the technology look sleek and modern?
Do most of my friends already use it?
Is it simply the cheapest option today?

diagnoses.3: Judges sustainability by present cost alone, ignoring long-term effects.

items.target: Account for local conditions in a plan
items.stem: A town in the North Georgia mountains wants to use solar power. Which local challenge must its energy plan address?
options: Solar panels only work right beside the ocean
There is never any usable sunlight in Georgia
Mountains and trees can shade the solar panels
Solar power cannot be used anywhere in Georgia

diagnoses.3: Assumes a source that works elsewhere cannot be adapted to local conditions.

items.target: One plan does not fit every location
items.stem: Why won't a single energy plan work for every location in the United States?
options: Only coal can realistically be used everywhere
All locations have exactly the same resources
Energy needs are identical in every location
Available resources differ from place to place

diagnoses.1: Believes all locations across the U.S. use the same energy resources.

items.target: Weigh trade-offs of a large project
items.stem: Before building a large hydropower dam, planners should carefully consider:
options: Only how tall and impressive the dam looks
Only the color of the reservoir's water
Cost, fish migration, and flooded farmland
Nothing — large dams have no real downsides

diagnoses.3: Believes large renewable projects have no environmental or social costs.

items.target: Features of a good local energy plan
items.stem: A good sustainable energy plan for a specific location is one that:
options: Fits reliable local resources to local needs
Uses the most polluting source it can find
Ignores the local geography completely
Copies another distant country's plan word for word

diagnoses.3: Assumes a plan can simply be copied without regard to local conditions.

items.stem: When excess nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer runs off farms into a lake, it often causes:
options: The water to become clearer and much healthier
The amount of oxygen for fish to increase a lot
Algal blooms that lower the water's oxygen
No measurable change at all to the water

diagnoses.1: Thinks nutrient runoff raises dissolved oxygen instead of depleting it.

items.stem: A student says human activities do not really affect natural resources. Which example best refutes this claim?
options: Only volcanoes ever affect our natural resources
Mining causes erosion and pollutes groundwater
Natural resources are basically unlimited for us
Human activities have no measurable effect at all

diagnoses.3: Believes human activities do not impact natural resources.
diagnoses.2: Believes natural resources are effectively unlimited.

items.stem: Nitrogen fertilizer from Midwest farms travels down the Mississippi River and helps create a low-oxygen 'dead zone' in the Gulf of Mexico. This is an example of:
options: An improvement in the Gulf's water quality
Farm runoff harming water far downstream
Something affecting only the farm's own soil
A natural process unrelated to human activity

diagnoses.2: Believes a human activity only affects its immediate location.

items.stem: Which pairing of a human activity and its impact is correct?
options: Urbanization tends to create cleaner rivers
Overfishing leads to larger fish populations
Urbanization adds runoff that pollutes water
Deforestation results in much less erosion

diagnoses.0: Believes only some, obvious human activities affect resources.

items.stem: Ocean acidification happens as the ocean absorbs excess CO₂, forming carbonic acid. Which statement is accurate?
options: The ocean has literally turned into an acid
The ocean is steadily becoming more basic
Carbon dioxide has no effect on ocean water
Ocean pH is dropping, harming shelled animals

diagnoses.0: Believes ocean acidification means the ocean has become an acid.

items.stem: Adding rooftop gardens and green spaces in a city most directly helps reduce:
options: The tilt of the Earth's axis in its orbit
The frequency of nearby volcanic eruptions
The daily rise and fall of the ocean tides
The urban heat island effect in cities

diagnoses.2: Applies a local urban solution to an unrelated global/geologic process.

items.stem: Which action most directly reduces photochemical smog?
options: Removing all of the trees from the city
Increasing overall fossil-fuel use in cities
Banning all rooftop and community gardens
Cutting emissions from vehicles and plants

diagnoses.1: Selects an action that increases the pollutants causing smog.

items.stem: A student says nothing can be done to reduce human impact on the environment. Which real example refutes this?
options: Using even more CFCs would help the ozone
Removing green spaces from all our cities
Nothing humans have ever tried has worked
Banning CFCs helped the ozone layer recover

diagnoses.2: Believes no solutions will work to reduce human impact.

items.stem: Growing the same crop on the same land year after year (monoculture) can lead to:
options: The soil growing richer and richer over time
Permanently high yields with no added inputs
Depleted soil that can slowly turn to desert
Greater and greater biodiversity in the soil

diagnoses.0: Believes repeated monoculture improves soil rather than depleting it.
diagnoses.1: Believes it is easy to keep increasing food supply indefinitely.

items.stem: The Green Revolution greatly increased grain yields worldwide. What is a major TRADE-OFF of these high-yield crops?
options: They out-produce native strains with no inputs
They require almost no water to grow well
They remove the need for farming altogether
They require heavy fertilizer and pesticide use

diagnoses.0: Believes high-yield strains always outperform native strains without added inputs.

items.stem: What is one purpose of genetically modified (GMO) crops?
options: To make the crops less nutritious than before
To deliberately shrink the world food supply
To let crops grow with no soil whatsoever
To add pest resistance or drought tolerance

diagnoses.0: Holds a purely negative misunderstanding of what GMOs are designed to do.

items.stem: Why do many farmers use crop rotation instead of continuous monoculture?
options: Different crops use and restore different nutrients
Because every crop needs the exact same nutrients
To use up and deplete the soil much faster
To intentionally trigger local desertification

diagnoses.1: Believes all crops draw the same nutrients, so rotation would make no difference.

items.stem: Compared with Less Developed Countries (LDCs), More Developed Countries (MDCs) generally have:
options: Higher income (GNP) and lower fertility rates
Nearly identical income and fertility rates
No formal system of public education at all
Lower average income and higher fertility rates

diagnoses.3: Reverses the relationship between development, income, and fertility.

items.target: Education affects fertility & quality of life
items.stem: Research shows that increasing access to education, especially for women, tends to:
options: Instantly erase every kind of human impact
Have no effect on population or quality of life
Sharply raise fertility rates across society
Lower fertility rates and improve quality of life

diagnoses.1: Believes education does not affect quality of life or population growth.

items.stem: The replacement fertility rate for humans is about 2.1 births per woman. A total fertility rate well ABOVE 2.1 suggests that a population is:
options: Growing in size
Having no children
Shrinking in size
Perfectly stable

diagnoses.2: Misreads a high fertility rate as causing population decline.

items.target: Development is linked to human impact
items.stem: Which statement about a nation's development and its impact on the environment is best supported?
options: Only less-developed countries harm the environment
Only highly-developed countries harm the planet
Development shapes quality of life and impact
A nation's development has no link to its impact

diagnoses.3: Believes the development of a nation does not affect its impact on Earth.

items.stem: A population increases in size when:
options: The birth and death rates are exactly equal
The death rate is higher than the birth rate
The birth rate is higher than the death rate
No individuals in the population are born

diagnoses.1: Reverses the relationship between birth rate, death rate, and growth.

items.stem: A population pyramid shaped like a wide-based triangle usually indicates a country with:
options: A shrinking population that is mostly elderly
A high fertility rate with many young people
Low fertility and a long life expectancy
An equal number at every age, with no pattern

diagnoses.0: Misinterprets a wide base (many young) as an aging, shrinking population.

items.stem: A student claims that all populations on Earth are growing at the same rate. Why is this incorrect?
options: No populations anywhere are actually growing
It is correct — growth is identical everywhere
Only the U.S. population ever really changes
Growth is uneven; rates differ by country

diagnoses.1: Believes all populations across the world grow at the same rate.

items.stem: A population pyramid shaped like a tall 'rocket' (fairly even width top to bottom) most likely represents a country with:
options: Only young children and no adults at all
No older people present in it at all
Low fertility, with both young and old present
Very high fertility and almost no elderly people at all

diagnoses.3: Confuses the even 'rocket' shape (low fertility) with a wide-based high-fertility pyramid.

items.stem: The factories of the Industrial Revolution greatly increased demand for which resource, adding pollution to the air?
options: None — factories used no energy
Only wind power from turbines
Coal and other fossil fuels
Sunlight captured by panels

diagnoses.0: Overlooks the enormous fossil-fuel demand created by industrialization.

items.stem: Advances in medicine (vaccines, surgery, disease control) affected human populations mainly by:
options: Having no effect on the size of populations
Raising life expectancy and growing population
Decreasing human life expectancy overall
Causing the total population to shrink

diagnoses.0: Believes technological/medical innovations do not affect population or impact.

items.stem: Agricultural innovations such as tractors and chemical fertilizers allowed:
options: Far less food to be grown than before
More food, fewer workers, but more fuel used
Farming to stop almost entirely everywhere
Food to be grown with no environmental effects

diagnoses.3: Believes new technologies carry no environmental cost.

items.stem: A student says new technologies never increase human impact on the environment. Which example best refutes this?
options: Engines and factories raised fuel use and smog
Technology only ever helps and never harms us
Technology carries no environmental cost at all
Innovations cut resource use all the way to zero

diagnoses.2: Believes new technologies do not increase human impact.

items.stem: Which individual action would most reduce a person's environmental impact?
options: Biking or taking the bus instead of driving alone
Throwing out items that could still be reused
Buying many more single-use plastic products
Leaving lights and devices switched on all day

diagnoses.3: Selects an action that increases, rather than reduces, energy use.

items.stem: A student says one person's choices cannot make any difference. Which idea best challenges this?
options: Recycling never actually helps anything
Small actions add up across many people
Only governments can affect the environment
One person truly cannot make any difference

diagnoses.3: Believes one person cannot make a difference.
diagnoses.2: Places all responsibility on governments, dismissing individual choices.

items.stem: How can market forces affect a person's ability to make sustainable choices?
options: Cost never influences a purchase decision
Prices and available options shape what we buy
Everything is always plastic-free and free
Market options and prices don't affect choices

diagnoses.3: Overlooks how market forces and cost constrain personal choices.

items.stem: Plastics that are thrown away improperly often end up as:
options: Useful nutrients that enrich garden soil
Harmless gases that leave no trace behind
Clean, safe drinking water for communities
Microplastics in oceans, water, and food

diagnoses.0: Believes discarded plastics harmlessly break down into soil nutrients.
